title: The log in the fire (Dark Night 2.10)
hook: wet wood hisses and blackens before it becomes flame

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Canticle: where have you hidden, and woods clothed in beauty. Your line was where have you hidden. What did you find outdoors? Today, John's most down-to-earth picture of the night. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

If you've ever built a campfire with damp wood, you know what happens. You wait for a big, cheerful flame. Instead you get hissing. Popping. Water bubbling out of the ends of the log. Clouds of gray smoke in your eyes. The bark goes black and ugly. It smells bad. It looks like the fire is ruining the wood, and you start to wonder if it'll ever catch. And then, slowly, it does. John of the Cross knew fires like that. Today's word is his picture.
screen: `A CAMPFIRE WITH DAMP WOOD.` → `HISSING, SMOKE, BLACKENED BARK.` → `THEN, SLOWLY, IT CATCHES.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. In the Dark Night, book two, chapter ten, John walks through it. When fire first touches a log, it doesn't set it ablaze. It starts by drying it, driving out the dampness, so the wood seems to weep. Then it blackens it, makes it dark and ugly, even gives off a bad smell. Only as it dries does the fire give it heat and light. And at the end, the wood becomes fire itself, as bright and hot as the flame. Second, the log is the soul. The fire is God's love. When that love first gets close, John says, the soul doesn't feel lit up. It feels worse. It suddenly sees its own damp and dark places, faults it didn't know it had. Third, the surprise. Here's John's key point. The fire isn't making the wood ugly. The ugliness was already in the wood. The fire is just drawing it out, so it can be burned away. So when someone who's trying to love God suddenly feels more aware of their failings, John says, that's often not a sign of getting worse. It's the smoke. It means the fire is working. Fourth, the flame. And the same fire that hurt at first becomes the one that delights. The log doesn't stay a log with a fire next to it. It becomes flame. John wrote a whole other poem about that end, the Living Flame of Love. So be patient with the smoke. Yours, and other people's.
screen: `DRYING, BLACKENING, THEN FLAME.` · `THE LOG IS THE SOUL.` · `THE FIRE DRAWS OUT WHAT WAS THERE.` · `THE WOOD BECOMES FIRE.` · then, large: `FIRST SMOKE, THEN FLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with your own smoke. Settle and breathe. Think of one fault you've been noticing in yourself lately, maybe more than before. Impatience, envy, a sharp tongue. Instead of beating yourself up, picture it as smoke rising off a log, damp coming out so it can burn clean. If you pray, you can let God's love keep working on it. If you don't, try just being gentle with yourself, the way you'd wait out a smoky fire. The bell holds the time.
The log in the fire. John's picture of the dark night: God's love first dries and blackens the soul, drawing out what's there, before it turns it into flame. Today's word.
screen: `THE LOG IN THE FIRE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: first smoke, then flame. Today, when someone near you is at their smoky worst, give them the patience you'd give damp wood. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors use John's image of the log in the fire to reassure people who feel more aware of their faults as they grow in prayer, and his Living Flame of Love is read as the fulfillment of that image.

original.note: Spanish: oh living flame of love. the first line of John's poem about the fire's end, when the wood becomes flame.

trapdoor: what you thought: a picture of suffering.
what it means: God's love first draws out what's damp and dark in the soul, then turns the whole soul into flame.
what a scholar hears: Dark Night 2.10; John reuses the image in the Living Flame of Love, where the same fire that purged now delights.

notes: Dark Night 2.10.1–3: the fire first dries the wood, makes it weep, blackens it, gives off a bad odor, then kindles and transforms it into fire; the soul sees its own miseries, which were already there. Paraphrased; confirm.
The same fire purging then delighting: Living Flame 1.19–25. Confirm reference.
The campfire scene is our illustration; the image itself is John's.
Original: first line of 'Llama de amor viva' is '¡Oh llama de amor viva,'; confirm.
